title: Every tasbih is charity
hookLine: the poor ask how to match the rich, and are told every glorification, praise and good word is charity (Nawawi 25, Abu Dharr)
tomorrow: your body owes something every morning. what, and to whom?

lines: THE RICH GET ALL THE REWARD.
cards: Click, click, click: prayer beads moving through a grandmother's fingers, one bead per phrase.
Meanwhile the fundraiser table, the donation link, the round-up at checkout can make giving feel like a club for people with money.
In al-Nawawi's twenty-fifth hadith, some poor companions come to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint that sounds very current. The wealthy have taken all the reward.
They pray as we pray, fast as we fast, and give charity from their extra money. So the poor say the rich get it all. What's the answer?

teach.h: HASN'T ALLAH GIVEN YOU THINGS TO GIVE?
teach.b: From Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: hasn't Allah given you things to give?
Every tasbih, saying subhanallah, glory be to Allah, is charity. Every takbir, Allahu akbar, is charity. Every alhamdulillah is charity.
Every la ilaha illallah is charity. Telling someone to do good is charity; stopping a wrong is charity. Look at what just happened.
A word, the cheapest thing a person owns, gets moved into the column of giving. The poor companions weren't told the rich were wrong to give.
They were handed a treasury they'd been carrying all along. Nobody has to wait for a paycheck to start giving. And this hadith runs on the ears.

teach.h: A SOUND, COUNTED AS A GIFT.
teach.b: A tasbih is a sound: a phrase said softly, often counted on beads or on the fingers, so the counting itself has a texture, bead after bead, joint after joint. The hadith treats that sound as currency.

Something to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, a whispered glory be to Allah sits in the same column as a gift of money. And the money isn't canceled either: give what you have, and add the words.

how: Many Muslims say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar after prayers, counting on prayer beads (a misbaha or tasbih) or on their fingers.

games.q: what does “every tasbih is charity” mean?
o: each word of praise to God counts as a gift
a weekly fee paid to keep the mosque open
a set of beads you must buy in order to pray

games.q: a treasury of words — tap the pairs.
p: felt the rich had all the reward

s: charity in Islam only means money
this hadith counts every tasbih, takbir and good word as charity.
telling someone to do good is listed as charity
the hadith tells the rich their giving doesn't count
the rich aren't faulted; the poor are shown what they already have to give.

games.q: your little sister says she can't give anything at Eid because she has no allowance. what does today's hadith hand her?
o: words count: a tasbih, a good word, stopping a wrong are charity.
nothing yet; charity means money, so she can give when she's older.
she should borrow some money so she can give like the adults do.
games.why: the poor companions had the same worry, and were handed a treasury of words they already carried.

practice: Say a short phrase of praise or thanks softly, again and again, at the pace of your breath, counting on the joints of your fingers. If you pray, subhanallah fits; if not, a plain thank you works.
Let a bead, or the press of a thumb on a knuckle, keep the time, and listen to the sound more than the count.

wordCard.voice: Every tasbih is charity: each word of glory, counted as a gift. The hadith's answer to people with no money to give.

orig.note: Arabic: charity, a gift freely given; in this hadith, stretched to cover words.

carryVoice: Keep this one: every glory is a gift, even the quietest one, said under your breath. Hadith twenty-five, said softly.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 25; Sahih Muslim 1006 (Abu Dharr)
